name: Galleon Drift
geological_features: A vast ring system with gaps carved by shepherd moons
Slow atmospheric circulation with wide, lazy cloud bands
A rocky-metallic core larger than most terrestrial planets
Trojan asteroid clusters at L4 and L5 points
specific_features: A derelict megastructure fragment orbiting within the ring system, origin unknown
description: Galleon Drift is the largest gas giant in its system, a colossus of hydrogen and helium whose massive ring system and lazy atmospheric circulation give it an air of stately calm that belies the crushing forces within. The cloud bands move with glacial slowness compared to smaller gas giants, their muted brown and cream tones creating a surface of subtle beauty. The ring system is the planet's crown — a broad, bright structure with sharply defined gaps maintained by a retinue of shepherd moons.

The atmosphere is predominantly hydrogen with significant helium and trace toxic compounds, standard for a gas giant of this mass. What sets Galleon Drift apart is its unusual calmness — atmospheric winds rarely exceed three hundred kilometers per hour, making it one of the least turbulent gas giants surveyed. This relative tranquility extends to its magnetosphere, which is powerful but stable, lacking the erratic fluctuations that make other gas giants hazardous to approach.

The megastructure fragment orbiting within the ring system was discovered forty years ago and has defied every attempt at identification. It is approximately eight kilometers long, constructed of materials that resist spectral analysis, and appears to be a section of something much larger that was either deliberately placed or became gravitationally captured. No similar materials or construction techniques appear in any known archaeological record, and the fragment's orbital parameters suggest it has been in its current position for at least a million years.

Galleon Drift's calm atmosphere and rich helium-3 reserves make it the preferred fuel source in the system, and scooping operations run continuously from a permanent orbital facility. The megastructure fragment has been placed off-limits pending further study, though salvage operators have been caught attempting unauthorized approaches more than once. The Trojan clusters at the L4 and L5 points host small mining communities that service the fuel operations and contribute to the slow, ongoing effort to understand what the fragment once was and who built it.
